lessons.title: Lab: Stoichiometry and theoretical oxygen demand

story.title: How much oxygen will the sugar eat?

scenes.text: A food factory discharges glucose-rich wash water. The regulator asks how much dissolved oxygen it would consume in the river.
Balanced chemical equations give the upper bound: the theoretical oxygen demand (ThOD).

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Write the complete oxidation of the compound to CO2, H2O (and NO3⁻ if nitrogen is oxidised).
2. Balance it.
3. ThOD (g O2/g compound) = (moles O2 × 32) ÷ (molar mass of compound).
The measured COD is usually close to ThOD for easily oxidised organics; BOD5 is lower because oxidation is biological and incomplete in 5 days.

steps.title: Worked example 1: glucose
steps.body:
C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O.
Molar mass = 180.16; O2 = 6 × 32 = 192.
ThOD = 192/180.16 = **1.066 g O2 per g glucose**.
For 100 mg/L glucose: 106.6 mg/L.

steps.title: Worked example 2: nitrification
steps.body:
NH4⁺ + 2 O2 → NO3⁻ + 2 H⁺ + H2O.
O2 per N = 64/14.01 = **4.57 g O2 per g NH4⁺-N**.
A wastewater with 25 mg/L NH4⁺-N therefore exerts a nitrogenous demand of about 114 mg/L O2, which is why ammonia is limited in effluents.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the mass of NH4⁺ instead of N as the basis.
- Not balancing hydrogen and oxygen on both sides.
- Equating BOD5 with ThOD; they differ.

lessons.title: Lab: pH, weak acids and buffers

story.title: The pond that would not stay neutral

scenes.text: After acidic discharge, one pond's pH barely moved while another crashed from 7 to 4.
The difference was buffer capacity from dissolved bicarbonate.

steps.title: Key relations
steps.body:
- pH = −log10[H⁺]; Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so pH + pOH = 14.
- Weak acid HA: Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. For C ≫ Ka, [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C).
- **Henderson–Hasselbalch**: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
- A buffer works best within pKa ± 1 and with high concentration.

steps.title: Worked example 1: weak acid
steps.body:
0.10 M acetic acid, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵.
[H⁺] = √(1.8×10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = √(1.8×10⁻⁶) = 1.34×10⁻³ M.
pH = **2.87**. (Check: x/C = 1.3 % < 5 %, so the approximation is valid.)

steps.title: Worked example 2: buffer
steps.body:
0.20 M sodium acetate + 0.10 M acetic acid. pKa = 4.74.
pH = 4.74 + log(0.20/0.10) = 4.74 + 0.301 = **5.04**.
Adding 0.01 mol/L strong acid converts 0.01 acetate to acetic acid: pH = 4.74 + log(0.19/0.11) = 4.98, a change of only 0.06.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using [H⁺] = C for weak acids.
- Averaging pH values directly (pH is logarithmic; average [H⁺]).
- Using HH equation with total concentrations far outside pKa ± 1.

lessons.title: Lab: Solubility product and precipitation

scenes.text: A town's tubewell water leaves scale in kettles. The plant operator raises pH with lime and watches white sludge settle.
Ksp tells us at what ion concentration a solid starts to form.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: For a salt MxAy ⇌ xM + yA, Ksp = [M]^x[A]^y at saturation. If the ion product Q > Ksp, precipitation occurs; Q < Ksp, dissolution. The **common-ion effect** lowers solubility; complexation raises it. Precipitation is used for hardness, phosphate (as FePO4/AlPO4) and heavy-metal removal as hydroxides.

steps.title: Worked example 2: Mg(OH)2 precipitation pH
steps.body:
Mg²⁺ = 100 mg/L = 100/24.31/1000 = 4.11×10⁻³ M; Ksp(Mg(OH)2) = 1.8×10⁻¹¹.
[OH⁻]² = 1.8×10⁻¹¹/4.11×10⁻³ = 4.37×10⁻⁹ → [OH⁻] = 6.6×10⁻⁵ M.
pOH = 4.18, so precipitation begins at **pH ≈ 9.82** — hence excess-lime softening at pH ≈ 10.5–11.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the exponent: for Mg(OH)2 the [OH⁻] term is squared.
- Using Ksp with concentrations in mg/L instead of mol/L.
- Ignoring ionic strength and complexes in real waters (activity ≠ concentration).

lessons.title: Lab: Reaction kinetics and temperature correction

story.title: Why the plant struggles in January

scenes.text: A treatment plant in north India removes less BOD in winter although nothing in the design changed.
Rate constants fall with temperature and the engineer must correct them.

steps.title: Rate laws
steps.body:
- Zero order: C = C0 − kt. First order: C = C0 e^(−kt); half-life t½ = ln2/k = 0.693/k. Second order: 1/C = 1/C0 + kt.
- Temperature: k_T = k_20 θ^(T−20), with θ ≈ 1.047 for BOD, 1.02–1.08 for biological processes, higher for chemical ones (Arrhenius: k = A e^(−Ea/RT)).
- Most environmental decay (BOD, disinfection Chick's law, radioactive decay, volatilisation) is first order.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A pollutant decays with k = 0.20 d⁻¹. t½ = 0.693/0.20 = **3.47 d**. After 10 d fraction left = e^(−2) = 0.135, i.e. 86.5 % removed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing log10-based and ln-based k (k_base10 = k_e/2.303).
- Applying θ-correction with T in kelvin instead of °C difference.
- Using first-order equations when concentration is not limiting enough (Monod kinetics at high substrate).

lessons.title: Lab: Hardness: carbonate and non-carbonate

scenes.text: A textile unit's boiler tubes scale up within months.
The chemist separates temporary from permanent hardness to choose a softening process.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Total hardness (TH) = Σ divalent cations (mainly Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺) in mg/L as CaCO3 = 2.497[Ca mg/L] + 4.118[Mg mg/L].
- **Carbonate hardness (CH)** = the part balanced by alkalinity: CH = min(TH, Alk).
- **Non-carbonate hardness (NCH)** = TH − Alk when TH > Alk; otherwise 0.
Classes (as CaCO3): soft < 60; moderately hard 60–120; hard 120–180; very hard > 180 mg/L.
EDTA titration with Eriochrome Black T at pH 10 measures TH.

steps.title: Worked example 2: EDTA
steps.body:
50 mL sample consumes 12.0 mL of 0.01 M EDTA (1 mol EDTA per mol Ca/Mg). Moles = 0.012 × 0.01 = 1.2×10⁻⁴ mol → ×100.09 g/mol = 12.0 mg CaCO3 in 50 mL.
TH = 12.0 mg / 0.050 L = **240 mg/L as CaCO3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling NCH negative when alkalinity exceeds hardness (then NCH = 0 and the excess alkalinity is Na/K bicarbonate).
- Omitting Fe, Mn, Sr when they are significant.
- Using EDTA without pH 10 buffer.

lessons.title: Lab: Dissolved oxygen and Henry's law

story.title: Fish kills in the summer lake

scenes.text: Dead fish appear at dawn in a warm, nutrient-rich lake.
Warm water holds less oxygen, and respiration at night uses it up.

steps.title: Gas solubility
steps.body:
Henry's law: C = K_H · p. For O2 in air at 25 °C, K_H ≈ 1.26×10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ atm⁻¹ and p(O2) = 0.2095 atm (dry air, ignoring water vapour).
Saturation DO at sea level (fresh water): 14.6 mg/L at 0 °C, 9.09 at 20 °C, 8.26 at 25 °C, 7.56 at 30 °C. It falls with temperature, salinity and altitude. Most fish need > 4–5 mg/L.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: C = 1.26×10⁻³ × 0.2095 = 2.64×10⁻⁴ mol/L × 32 000 mg/mol = **8.45 mg/L** (about 8.26 after correcting for water-vapour pressure).

steps.title: Worked example 2: altitude
steps.body: At an altitude where pressure is 0.70 atm, saturation at 20 °C ≈ 9.09 × 0.70 = **6.4 mg/L** (approximately, ignoring vapour-pressure refinement). A plant designed with sea-level oxygen transfer must be re-rated.

steps.body:
- Using total pressure instead of O2 partial pressure.
- Assuming DO > saturation is impossible (algae can supersaturate by day).
- Forgetting the 32 g/mol conversion.

lessons.title: Lab: BOD test and kinetics

scenes.text: A dairy's effluent sample goes in a 20 °C incubator for five days.
The drop in dissolved oxygen is the BOD.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body:
BOD is oxygen used by microbes to oxidise biodegradable organics. First-order model: **BOD_t = L0 (1 − e^(−kt))**, L0 = ultimate carbonaceous BOD, k ≈ 0.23 d⁻¹ (base e) at 20 °C for domestic sewage (0.1 d⁻¹ base 10). BOD5 is roughly 68 % of L0 for k = 0.23.
**Dilution method**: BOD = (DO_i − DO_f)/P, P = sample volume ÷ bottle volume. Use dilutions giving DO depletion ≥ 2 mg/L and residual DO ≥ 1 mg/L. Seed the sample if it lacks microbes; add nitrification inhibitor to measure carbonaceous BOD.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using bottles with < 2 mg/L depletion or < 1 mg/L residual DO.
- Ignoring the seed correction.
- Quoting BOD5 as ultimate BOD.

steps.title: Chapman cycle and catalysis
steps.body:
O2 + hν (λ < 242 nm) → 2 O; O + O2 + M → O3 + M; O3 + hν (λ ≈ 200–320 nm) → O2 + O; O + O3 → 2 O2.
Catalytic destruction by X = Cl, Br, NO, OH: X + O3 → XO + O2; XO + O → X + O2; net O3 + O → 2 O2. One Cl atom may destroy ~10⁵ ozone molecules.
CFC-12 (CF2Cl2) + UV → CF2Cl + Cl. Over Antarctica, polar stratospheric clouds convert reservoirs (HCl, ClONO2) into Cl2, which photolyses in spring sunlight.

steps.title: Worked example 1: photon energy
steps.body: E = hc/λ = (6.626×10⁻³⁴ × 3.0×10⁸)/(242×10⁻⁹) = 8.21×10⁻¹⁹ J per photon. Per mole × 6.022×10²³ = **494 kJ/mol**, about the O=O bond energy (498 kJ/mol).

steps.title: Worked example 2: Dobson units
steps.body: 1 DU = 0.01 mm of pure O3 at STP. Normal column ≈ 300 DU = 3 mm; the 'hole' threshold is < 220 DU.

steps.body:

- Saying UV-C reaches the ground (it is absorbed; UV-B partially).

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body:

VOCs form peroxy radicals (RO2•) that convert NO to NO2 without consuming ozone, so O3 accumulates. Products: O3, PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate), aldehydes, HNO3.
Conditions: sunlight, NOx, VOCs, stagnation, inversion. Control: reduce NOx and VOC (catalytic converters, fuel standards).

steps.title: Worked example 1

steps.title: Groups of microorganisms
steps.body:
- **Bacteria and Archaea**: prokaryotes, no membrane-bound nucleus, 70S ribosomes, 0.5–5 µm; archaea include methanogens.
- **Fungi** (yeasts, moulds), **algae**, **protozoa**: eukaryotes with nucleus, organelles, 80S ribosomes, 5–100+ µm.
- **Viruses**: 20–300 nm, nucleic acid in a protein coat, obligate parasites, not cells.
Bacterial shapes: cocci (spheres), bacilli (rods), spirilla/vibrios (spirals/commas). Reproduction: binary fission.

steps.title: Gram stain: why it matters
steps.body: Steps: crystal violet → iodine → alcohol wash → safranin. **Gram-positive** cells (thick peptidoglycan) stay purple; **Gram-negative** (thin peptidoglycan plus outer membrane) lose the violet and appear pink. Coliforms, Salmonella and Vibrio are Gram-negative; Bacillus and Staphylococcus are Gram-positive.

steps.title: Worked example: scale
steps.body: A 2 µm E. coli cell is 2000 nm; a 100 nm virus is 20 times smaller, so it passes through a 0.45 µm membrane filter that retains bacteria.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

steps.title: Phases
steps.body:
1. **Lag**: adaptation, no net growth.
2. **Exponential (log)**: N = N0·2^n, n = t/g; ln N linear in t.
3. **Stationary**: growth = death; nutrient limitation.
4. **Death/decline**: exponential decrease.
Generation (doubling) time g; specific growth rate µ = ln 2 / g. E. coli g ≈ 20 min in rich medium, 30–60 min in water-treatment conditions; nitrifiers 10–50 h.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: N0 = 1000 cells/mL, g = 30 min, t = 5 h → n = 10 generations. N = 1000 × 2¹⁰ = **1.02×10⁶ cells/mL**.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Time to rise from 10³ to 10⁶: n = log2(1000) = 9.97 generations; t = 9.97 × 30 = **299 min ≈ 5 h**. µ = 0.693/0.5 h = 1.39 h⁻¹.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ln instead of log2 for number of generations.
- Applying exponential growth in the stationary phase.
- Mixing units of g (min) and µ (h⁻¹).

steps.title: Equations
steps.body:
**Monod**: µ = µmax·S/(Ks + S). Ks = substrate concentration where µ = µmax/2.
Yield: Y = ΔX/ΔS (g biomass per g substrate), typical heterotrophs Y ≈ 0.4–0.6 g VSS/g BOD; nitrifiers 0.1–0.2.
Growth with decay: net µ_net = µ − kd (endogenous decay kd ≈ 0.05–0.1 d⁻¹).
Substrate utilisation rate: r_su = −µmax X S/(Y (Ks + S)).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: µmax = 6 d⁻¹, Ks = 20 mg/L, S = 10 mg/L: µ = 6 × 10/30 = **2.0 d⁻¹**. At S = 20: 3.0 d⁻¹ (half of max).

steps.title: Worked example 2: biomass produced
steps.body: Y = 0.5, kd = 0.06 d⁻¹, µ = 2.0 d⁻¹ → net µ = **1.94 d⁻¹**. Removing 200 mg/L BOD produces ΔX = 0.5 × 200 = 100 mg/L VSS (before decay).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating Ks as a rate rather than a concentration.
- Applying Monod beyond substrate-limited conditions (inhibition at toxic concentrations needs Haldane).
- Forgetting decay when computing net sludge production.

- **Enzymes**: protein catalysts; Michaelis–Menten v = Vmax S/(Km + S); denature at high temperature and extreme pH.

lessons.title: Lab: Nitrogen cycle, nitrification and denitrification

story.title: The ammonia that would not go away

scenes.text: A sewage plant meets its BOD limit but its effluent ammonia still exceeds the permit.
Slow-growing nitrifiers had been washed out of the aeration tank.

steps.title: Pathways
steps.body:
- **Ammonification**: organic N → NH4⁺.
- **Nitrification** (aerobic, autotrophic): NH4⁺ + 1.5 O2 → NO2⁻ + 2H⁺ + H2O (*Nitrosomonas*); NO2⁻ + 0.5 O2 → NO3⁻ (*Nitrobacter*). Overall NH4⁺ + 2O2 → NO3⁻ + 2H⁺ + H2O.
- **Denitrification** (anoxic, heterotrophic): 2NO3⁻ + 10e⁻ + 12H⁺ → N2 + 6H2O, using organic carbon.
- **Fixation**: N2 → NH3 (Rhizobium, cyanobacteria, Azotobacter).
Stoichiometry: nitrification uses **7.14 mg alkalinity (as CaCO3) per mg NH4⁺-N** and 4.57 mg O2; denitrification returns about **3.57 mg alkalinity per mg NO3⁻-N** and saves 2.86 mg O2 equivalent.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Nitrify 30 mg/L NH4⁺-N: O2 = 30 × 4.57 = **137 mg/L**; alkalinity used = 30 × 7.14 = **214 mg/L as CaCO3**. If influent alkalinity is only 200 mg/L, pH will crash unless alkali is added.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Denitrifying 20 mg/L NO3⁻-N recovers 20 × 3.57 = 71 mg/L alkalinity and needs about 2.86 mg BOD per mg N, i.e. 57 mg/L BOD.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing nitrification (aerobic) with denitrification (anoxic).
- Ignoring that nitrifiers need long solids retention time (> 8–10 d at 20 °C) and DO > 2 mg/L.
- Forgetting temperature and pH sensitivity (best pH 7.5–8.5).

steps.title: Four stages
steps.body:
1. **Hydrolysis**: polymers → sugars, amino acids, fatty acids.
2. **Acidogenesis**: → volatile fatty acids, H2, CO2.
3. **Acetogenesis**: VFAs → acetate, H2, CO2.
4. **Methanogenesis**: acetate → CH4 + CO2 (acetoclastic, ~70 % of CH4); CO2 + 4H2 → CH4 + 2H2O (hydrogenotrophic).
Theoretical yield: **0.35 m³ CH4 per kg COD destroyed at STP (0 °C, 1 atm)**; at 35 °C ≈ 0.395 m³/kg. Biogas ≈ 60–65 % CH4. Sulphate-reducing bacteria compete: SO4²⁻ + 8e⁻ → H2S (corrosion, odour).
Optimum: mesophilic 35 °C or thermophilic 55 °C, pH 6.8–7.4, alkalinity 2000–5000 mg/L.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A UASB removes 1000 kg COD/day. CH4 at STP = 1000 × 0.35 = **350 m³/day**; at 35 °C = 350 × 308/273 = 395 m³/day. With 65 % CH4 the biogas is about 600 m³/day.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Neglecting temperature of the gas volume.
- Digester failure from VFA accumulation (low pH inhibits methanogens).

steps.title: Indicators and diseases
steps.body:
Testing for each pathogen is slow and costly, so we test **indicators** that live in the gut: total coliforms, thermotolerant (faecal) coliforms and *E. coli* (the best indicator), faecal streptococci/enterococci. Desired: absent in 100 mL of drinking water (WHO and IS 10500).
Waterborne diseases: cholera (*Vibrio cholerae*), typhoid (*Salmonella* Typhi), bacillary dysentery (*Shigella*), hepatitis A/E (viruses), giardiasis, cryptosporidiosis (protozoa; cysts resist chlorine).
**MPN multiple-tube**: presumptive (lactose broth, gas at 35 °C/48 h) → confirmed (brilliant green bile broth) → completed. **Thomas formula**: MPN/100 mL = P × 100 / √(V_neg × V_all), P = number of positive tubes, V_neg = mL of sample in negative tubes, V_all = mL in all tubes. Alternative: membrane filtration, defined-substrate tests.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: 5 tubes × 10 mL: 3 positive. V_all = 50, V_neg = 20. MPN = 3 × 100/√(20 × 50) = 300/31.6 = **9.5 per 100 mL** (standard tables give 9.2).

steps.title: Worked example 2: interpretation
steps.body: Result 9.5 coliforms/100 mL fails drinking-water standards (should be 0) but may be acceptable for bathing water in some classes; action: boil/chlorinate, locate contamination (soak pit nearby).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating coliform presence as proof of a specific pathogen.
- Forgetting indicators do not represent protozoa and viruses well.
- Reading gas after the incubation limit (false positives).

lessons.title: Lab: Disinfection kinetics (Chick–Watson)

story.title: How long must the chlorine contact tank be?

scenes.text: A designer must guarantee a four-log kill before water leaves the plant.
Contact time and disinfectant dose both matter.

steps.title: Models
steps.body:
**Chick's law**: dN/dt = −kN → N/N0 = e^(−kt). Log removal = −log10(N/N0) = kt/2.303.
**Chick–Watson**: ln(N/N0) = −k′ Cⁿ t. **CT** = concentration × contact time (mg·min/L).
Factors: disinfectant type (O3 > ClO2 > HOCl > OCl⁻ > chloramine in power), pH (HOCl pKa 7.54), temperature, turbidity (shielding), organism (viruses and cysts resist more than vegetative bacteria).
Typical: free chlorine residual ≥ 0.2 mg/L at the end of the distribution (IS 10500 desirable 0.2 mg/L).

steps.title: Worked example 2: HOCl fraction
steps.body: At pH 7.54 half the free chlorine is HOCl; at pH 8.5 the HOCl fraction = 1/(1 + 10^(8.5−7.54)) = 1/(1 + 9.1) = **9.9 %**, so disinfection is about ten times slower for equal CT unless extra chlorine is applied.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating 99 % kill as 'sterile'.
- Ignoring chlorine demand before residual forms.

lessons.title: Lab: Sort the waste stream (sources and classification)

scenes.text: A municipal engineer is asked to audit one ward: households, markets, hotels, a hospital and a small factory all put waste on the same street.
Before any treatment is designed, every item must be placed in the right stream.

steps.title: Definitions and sources
steps.body:
**Solid waste** is any discarded solid or semi-solid material from human and animal activity that is no longer wanted. **Municipal solid waste (MSW)** covers residential, commercial, institutional, street-sweeping and market waste, excluding industrial process waste, bio-medical waste and hazardous waste, which are regulated separately.

Main sources: residential, commercial (shops, hotels, offices), institutional (schools, offices), municipal services (street sweepings, drain silt, park waste), construction and demolition (C&D), industrial, agricultural and healthcare.

steps.title: Classification by nature
steps.body:
- **Biodegradable (wet):** kitchen and food waste, vegetable market waste, garden waste, which are broken down by microbes.
- **Non-biodegradable recyclable (dry):** paper, cardboard, plastics, metals, glass, textiles.
- **Inert:** dust, ash, stones, construction debris, which are neither biodegradable nor usefully recyclable.
- **Hazardous:** batteries, paints, solvents, CFL tubes, pesticides containers, e-waste, sanitary and bio-medical items.

The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 require generators to segregate at source into three streams: wet (biodegradable), dry (non-biodegradable) and domestic hazardous waste (including sanitary waste, wrapped securely).

steps.title: Worked example: typical Indian composition
steps.body:
A ward survey of 2,000 kg gives: food and vegetable 1,000 kg, paper 240 kg, plastics 160 kg, glass and metal 100 kg, inert 400 kg, other 100 kg.

1. Food/vegetable fraction = 1000/2000 = 50%.
2. Biodegradable fraction (food) = 50%.
3. Recyclable dry (paper + plastic + glass/metal) = 500/2000 = 25%.

So half of the ward waste is compostable and a quarter is directly recyclable, which shapes the plant design: composting/biogas first, an MRF second.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling all plastic 'non-recyclable': many plastics (PET, HDPE) are recyclable, multilayer sachets are the problem.
- Mixing sanitary napkins and diapers with dry recyclables: they are domestic hazardous waste in the 2016 Rules and contaminate paper.
- Confusing MSW with hazardous or bio-medical waste, which have their own Rules.

lessons.title: Lab: Estimate waste generation and project growth

scenes.text: A town of 250,000 people plans a new waste plant that must serve until 2036.
The engineer needs today's tonnage and the projected per-capita rate.

steps.title: Generation rate
steps.body:
**Per-capita generation** is the mass of waste produced per person per day (kg/cap/day). Indian cities range from about 0.2–0.6 kg/cap/day, rising with income and city size. Total daily waste = population × per-capita rate. Rates grow with urbanisation, packaging and income; use a compound growth rate when projecting: **q_n = q_0 (1 + i)^n**.

Generation is measured by weighing vehicle loads at the weighbridge or by household surveys over at least a week, covering weekdays and weekends and wet and dry seasons.

steps.title: Worked example 1: today's tonnage
steps.body:
Population 250,000; rate 0.45 kg/cap/day.

1. Daily waste = 250,000 × 0.45 = 112,500 kg/day.
2. = **112.5 t/day**.
3. Annual = 112.5 × 365 = 41,062.5 t/year.

steps.title: Worked example 2: projected rate
steps.body:
Per-capita rate grows 1.5% per year for 10 years.

1. (1.015)^10 = 1.1605.
2. q_10 = 0.45 × 1.1605 = 0.522 kg/cap/day.
3. If population also reaches 300,000, waste = 300,000 × 0.522 = 156.7 t/day, a 39% rise on today.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing kg and tonnes: 112,500 kg is 112.5 t, not 1,125 t.
- Using simple instead of compound growth over long periods.
- Designing for average generation: plants need a design margin (peak days, festivals, monsoon moisture).

lessons.title: Lab: Physical characterisation — moisture, density and composition

story.title: Why the compost heap is soggy

steps.title: Key physical properties
steps.body:
- **Moisture content (wet basis):** (wet mass − dry mass)/wet mass × 100, with drying at 105 °C to constant mass. Indian MSW is typically 40–60% moisture.
- **Bulk (loose) density:** mass per unit volume. Uncompacted MSW is about 150–300 kg/m3; compacted in a truck 400–600 kg/m3.
- **Particle size and composition:** by manual sorting and sieving.

High moisture lowers calorific value and makes combustion difficult; high density lowers transport cost per tonne.

steps.title: Worked example: moisture
steps.body:
A 100 kg wet sample dries at 105 °C to 62 kg.

1. Water lost = 100 − 62 = 38 kg.
2. Moisture (wet basis) = 38/100 × 100 = **38%**.
3. On a dry basis the same sample is 38/62 = 61%. Always state the basis.

steps.title: Worked example: mixture calorific value
steps.body:
Composition and heating values: food 50% at 4,000 kJ/kg, paper 20% at 16,000, plastics 10% at 32,000, others 20% at 0.

HV = 0.5×4,000 + 0.2×16,000 + 0.1×32,000 = 2,000 + 3,200 + 3,200 = **8,400 kJ/kg**.

Only plastics and paper give energy; wet food waste mostly lowers it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Quoting moisture without stating wet or dry basis.
- Drying above 105 °C, which loses volatile organics.
- Taking a single grab sample instead of a representative one.

lessons.title: Lab: Chemical characterisation — ultimate analysis and the Dulong formula

scenes.text: A developer wants to burn refuse to generate power and asks for the heating value.
The lab reports carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and sulphur percentages.

steps.title: Proximate and ultimate analysis
steps.body:
**Proximate analysis** gives moisture, volatile matter, fixed carbon and ash. **Ultimate analysis** gives the elemental percentages of C, H, O, N, S (and ash) on a dry basis. Heating value can be measured in a bomb calorimeter or estimated from ultimate analysis by the **Dulong formula**:

**HHV (kJ/kg) = 337 C + 1428 (H − O/8) + 9 S**, with C, H, O, S in mass percent.

The term (H − O/8) is the 'available hydrogen' after some hydrogen is assumed combined with oxygen as water.

steps.title: Worked example: Dulong
steps.body:
Dry waste: C 48%, H 6.4%, O 37.6%, S 0.4%.

1. 337 × 48 = 16,176.
2. O/8 = 4.7; H − O/8 = 1.7; 1,428 × 1.7 = 2,427.6.
3. 9 × 0.4 = 3.6.
4. HHV = 16,176 + 2,427.6 + 3.6 = **18,607 kJ/kg** (dry).

For wet waste, multiply by (1 − moisture fraction), and subtract latent heat of the water to get the lower heating value.

steps.title: Worked example: from dry to as-received
steps.body:
Waste with 40% moisture, dry HHV 18,607 kJ/kg.

1. Dry fraction = 0.60.
2. As-received HHV ≈ 18,607 × 0.60 = 11,164 kJ/kg (before correcting for water vapour).
3. LHV ≈ HHV − 2,440 × (mass of water per kg incl. combustion water). The water of the 40% moisture alone costs 0.40 × 2,440 ≈ 976 kJ/kg, so LHV is roughly 10,190 kJ/kg ignoring combustion water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using fractions instead of percentages in Dulong.
- Using HHV where LHV is needed for boiler efficiency.
- Forgetting that wet Indian MSW often has an LHV below 7,000 kJ/kg, marginal for plain incineration.

story.title: Four heaps at the transfer yard

steps.title: Sampling by coning and quartering
steps.body: A representative sample must reflect the heterogeneity of the load. Method: heap the waste into a cone, flatten it, divide into four quarters, discard two opposite quarters, mix the remaining two and repeat until about 20–25 kg remain. Collect loads from different days and vehicles, avoid scavenged or wet-spot loads, and record date, weather and source.

steps.title: Proximate analysis procedure
steps.body:
1. **Moisture:** dry at 105 °C to constant mass.
2. **Volatile matter:** heat dry sample in covered crucible at about 950 °C for a fixed time and weigh the loss.
3. **Ash:** burn in open crucible at 550–950 °C to constant mass (the temperature depends on the method).
4. **Fixed carbon:** by difference = 100 − moisture − VM − ash.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
200 g wet sample: after 105 °C, 120 g; after covered heating at 950 °C, 55 g; after burning in air, 20 g ash.

1. Moisture = 80/200 = 40%.
2. VM = (120 − 55)/200 = 32.5%.
3. Ash = 20/200 = 10%.
4. Fixed carbon = 100 − 40 − 32.5 − 10 = **17.5%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Discarding the wrong quarters (they must be opposite).
- Wearing no gloves or mask when sorting: use PPE and vaccinate where advised.
- Reporting VM without specifying basis.

lessons.title: Lab: Size a community storage bin

story.title: The overflowing bin on Gandhi Road

scenes.text: Residents of 500 people share one community bin that is collected every second day, and it overflows every morning.
The engineer recomputes the required volume.

steps.title: Storage principles
steps.body:
**Primary storage** is at the source: household bins, colour-coded dust-bins (green for wet, blue for dry is the common Indian practice), and community bins. A bin must be sized for waste generated between two collections plus a safety factor, be covered, rodent-proof, easy to empty and located so that it is accessible but not a nuisance.

**Volume = (population × per-capita rate × collection interval) / bulk density**, with a safety factor of about 1.2–1.5.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
500 people × 0.4 kg/cap/day = 200 kg/day. Collection every 2 days = 400 kg. Bulk density 200 kg/m3.

1. Volume = 400/200 = **2 m3**.
2. With a 1.25 safety factor = 2.5 m3.
3. Choose standard bins: for example three 1.1 m3 containers (3.3 m3) or one 3 m3 skip.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring collection interval: missed pickups double the load.
- Using compacted density for storage bins (waste in bins is loose).
- Placing bins on road edges that block traffic or drains.

steps.title: Systems
steps.body:
- **Door-to-door:** waste collected from each household by workers with handcarts, tricycles or small tippers; best for source segregation.
- **Community bin (stationary container):** residents bring waste to bins, emptied by compactor trucks or tippers.
- **Hauled container system (HCS):** a loaded container is hauled to disposal and an empty one is left; suits large generators such as markets.
- **Stationary container system (SCS):** containers remain in place and are emptied into a collection vehicle.

**Secondary collection** moves waste from bins and transfer points to the plant or landfill.

steps.title: Worked example: HCS trips
steps.body:
Per trip: pick-up time 10 min, haul 2 × 20 min = 40 min, unloading 8 min, at-site time 5 min = 63 min. Shift 8 h with 30 min non-productive time.

Productive time = 480 − 30 = 450 min. Trips/day = 450/63 = 7.14, so **7 trips**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the same system everywhere: narrow lanes need small vehicles.
- Ignoring non-productive time (breaks, traffic).
- Allowing mixed loads in compartmented vehicles, defeating segregation.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Vehicles required = daily waste / (vehicle capacity × trips per vehicle per day × loading factor). Add 10–20% standby for maintenance. Round up, never down.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Waste 60 t/day; vehicle capacity 4 t; 2 trips per shift; loading factor 1.

1. Capacity per vehicle per day = 4 × 2 = 8 t.
2. Vehicles = 60/8 = 7.5, so **8** vehicles.
3. Add 15% standby: 8 × 1.15 = 9.2, so 10 vehicles in the fleet.

steps.title: Worked example: waste per trip
steps.body: A compactor with 5 m3 body, compacted density 500 kg/m3 carries 2,500 kg = 2.5 t per trip. Daily waste of 50 t needs 20 trips; with 4 trips per vehicle that is 5 vehicles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rounding 7.5 down to 7.
- Using rated capacity without a loading factor.
- Forgetting standby vehicles.

lessons.title: Lab: Transfer-station economics

scenes.text: The new landfill is 30 km from the city centre.
Small trucks driving all the way are costing a fortune.

steps.title: Why transfer stations
steps.body: A **transfer station** is an intermediate facility where waste from small collection vehicles is consolidated into large trucks or rail containers for long haul. It is economical beyond a break-even haul distance (often 15–25 km), cuts traffic and fuel, and allows compaction, sorting and weighing. Design for tipping hall, ramp, compactor or push pit, odour and leachate control and a washdown area.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Direct haul: 4 t truck at ₹30/km, round trip 60 km → ₹1,800 per trip → ₹450/t.

Transfer: station cost ₹150/t; large truck 20 t at ₹50/km × 60 km = ₹3,000 per trip → ₹150/t. Total = ₹300/t.

Saving = 450 − 300 = **₹150 per tonne**. At 100 t/day, ₹15,000/day or about ₹55 lakh a year.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing a transfer station near homes without odour control.
- Ignoring the extra handling cost.
- Choosing it for short hauls where it adds cost.
